hero.caption:
The Red Castle Museum, also known as Assaraya Alhamra Museum (Arabic: متحف السرايا الحمراء‎‎) or the Archaeological Museum of Tripoli, is a national museum in Libya. It is located in the historic building known as the Red Castle or Red Saraya.
Designed in conjunction with UNESCO, the museum covers 5,000 years from prehistory to the independence revolution (1953) era.[1] It is located in Tripoli's Assaria al-Hamra or Red Castle fortress, on the promontory above and adjacent to the old-town district with medina Ghadema. The museum has an entrance on historic As-Saha al-Kradrah, the Martyrs' Square.[2]

images.caption:
A circa 1950-1960 image of Independence Square (1950s-1960s) - on the harbour in downtown Tripoli, during the Libyan monarchy era.
The present day Martyrs' Square or "Maidan Al Shohdaa" , in independent Libya.
Aerial view is to the southwest, with Tripoli Bay in the foreground of the corniche and the two monument columns (before 1960s landfills extended land far into the harbour-bay).
The Ottoman era Red Castle (Tripoli Castle museum) is on the upper right, and former Teatro Miramareon the square's lower left.
Also formerly named Italian colonial Piazza Italia (1930s-1950s), and Green Square or "E'saha ElKhadra" (1970s-mid 2011).

images.caption:
The eastern side of Tripoli Castle
Tripoli Castle

Built by the Crusaders in the early 12th century on the ruins of a natural hill known as Hill of Pilgrims during the siege of the city located at that time on the coast, three kilometers from its current location. The Crusaders used it as a residence and a center for launching their military campaigns through a passageway/crypt that connected the castle to the Tripoli coast. The French Count Raymond de Saint-Gilles died there in 1105 AD following a battle that broke out between him and the city's ruler at the time, Jalal al-Malik bin Ammar, the Fatimid state's representative in ruling the country on behalf of the country. The Mamluks burned this castle in 1289 AD so that the Crusaders would not be able to regain control of the city. It was then rebuilt between 1307 and 1308 during the reign of Prince Asendemir Kurji, the city's ruler at the time, and was restored in 1521 AD during the reign of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. In the late Ottoman rule, the Turks turned it into a prison. The castle went through difficult days, as gangs and parties took turns controlling it during the Lebanese sectarian war, before its ownership returned to the Lebanese state.
